8658.t: BM3766: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Laboratory
8658.b:
Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3766 : Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

1. Implementation of Uninformed Search Algorithms (BFS, DFS): Implement basic uninformed search algorithms like Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) for problem-solving in search spaces.
2. Implementation of Informed Search Algorithms (A, Memory-Bounded A)**: Explore heuristic-based search techniques by implementing informed algorithms such as A* and memory-bounded A* for optimal pathfinding.
3. Implement Naïve Bayes Models: Build and test Naïve Bayes classifiers for probabilistic prediction, particularly useful for text classification and spam detection tasks.
4. Implement Bayesian Networks: Construct Bayesian networks to model complex probabilistic dependencies and perform inference tasks in domains with uncertainty.
5. Build Regression Models: Implement regression techniques (linear, polynomial, etc.) to predict continuous outcomes and analyze relationships between variables.
6. Build Decision Trees and Random Forests: Develop decision tree and random forest models for classification and regression, exploring concepts like feature importance and ensemble learning.
7. Build SVM (Support Vector Machine) Models: Implement Support Vector Machines for classification tasks, with an emphasis on understanding hyperplanes, kernels, and margin maximization.
8. Implement Ensembling Techniques: Apply ensembling methods like bagging, boosting, and stacking to improve the accuracy and robustness of machine learning models.
9. Implement Clustering Algorithms: Explore unsupervised learning by implementing clustering algorithms such as k-means and hierarchical clustering for grouping unlabeled data.
10. Implement EM (Expectation-Maximization) for Bayesian Networks: Apply the Expectation-Maximization algorithm to Bayesian networks to estimate parameters in cases with hidden data or incomplete datasets.
11. Build Simple Neural Network (NN) Models: Construct and train basic neural network models for tasks like image recognition or binary classification, focusing on feedforward and backpropagation processes.
12. Build Deep Learning Neural Network Models: Develop deeper neural network architectures, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) or Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), for more complex tasks in image processing, sequence prediction, or natural language processing.

Course Objective

1 .

Develop Competency in Machine Learning Algorithms and Models
2 .

Gain Practical Experience in Advanced Machine Learning Techniques and Model Ensembles
3 .

Build and Deploy Neural Network Models for Data-Driven Applications

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of this course, the student will be able to:
1. Understand basics concepts related to deep learning.
2. Understand the different types of deep neural network architectures.
3. Develop deep learning models for classification and regression tasks related to healthcare applications.
4. Develop deep learning models for time series prediction, risk estimation for healthcare applications.
5. Optimise neural network models for improving accuracy and performance.

Essential Reading

Aurelien Geron, Hands-On Machine Learning with Sci-kit Learn, Keras and Tensorflow, O'Reilly , First Edition

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CH6235 : Resource Recovery From Waste { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Introduction to waste production in different sectors such as domestic, industrial and agriculture etc. What is Waste? Waste Management Hierarchy and 3R Principle of Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. Waste minimization –reducing waste generation at source. Principles of Waste Utilization and introduction waste as a resource and recovery of this resource from waste. Types of waste (organic, inorganic, hazardous, infectious etc.). Characterization & Classification of waste –agrobased, forest residues, industrial waste (hazardous and non-hazardous), municipal solid waste, plastic waste, biomedical waste, e-waste etc. Concept of–Zero Waste–Zero Pollution–Zero Landfill Three general methods of attaining zero pollution. Economics of zero pollution.
Technologies for Waste Utilization and cleaner production processes–aerobic digestion and anaerobic digestion composting, vermin-composting, briquetting/pelletization. Waste-to-Energy –combustion, gasification, pyrolysis, biomethanation, bio-refineries. Landfill gas generation, collection conversion to fuels for useful energy applications-engine, compressors, burners, lamps etc. Waste recycling to recover resources –Value added chemicals from acid gas, novel adsorbents from fly-ash, red mud etc. Clean Technologies and their applications in production processes.
Case studies & Success Stories of waste utilization in different industrial sectors: Manufacturing process, pollution sources, waste characterization, waste reduction/reuse/recovery and final treatment methods for–Pulp and Paper, Sugar, Distillery, Tannery, Dairy, Textile, Cement Manufacture, Thermal Power Plant, Dye and Dye Intermediates, pharmaceuticals and any other industry of importance.

1 .

At the end of the course the students are expected to be able to define and describe waste, its categories, the waste chain, the situation in flanders, hazardous waste, the waste hierarchy.
2 .

At the end of the course the students are expected to be able to describe, explain the principles, and other relevant aspects of waste recycling, recovery and reuse
3 .

At the end of the course the students are expected to be able to select the best treatment option for a given waste/rest stream
4 .

At the end of the course the students are expected to be able to explain the environmental implications of each treatment.

1 .

After completing the course, the students should be able to:
(1) Describe and analyze waste streams in terms of resource recovery
(2) Identify and describe suitable resource recovery processes from waste streams
(3) Compare and evaluate sustainable resource recovery processes from waste streams

Subject {L-T-P / C} : MM4504 : High Temperature Materials { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module 1) Introduction- Problem with materials at high temperature, Background: Time-dependent deformation Difference between ambient and elevated temperature plastic deformation. 06 Hrs
Module 2) Theories of Creep: Definition of creep Different methods of creep testing Creep curve Effect of stress and temperature on creep curve Effect of microstructure on creep Stress-rupture tests Difference between creep and stress-rupture test Superplasticity. 10 hrs
Module 3) Mechanism of creep deformation - Lattice mechanism - Dislocation glide, dislocation climb, Boundary mechanism-Nabarro-Herring, Coble, Grain boundary sliding Determination of stress exponent and activation energy for steady-state creep Creep fracture micro-mechanisms Creep behavior of nanocrystalline materials. 08 Hrs
Module 4) Deformation mechanism maps Presentation of engineering creep data-Monkman -Grant relationship, Larson-Millar parameter. 04 Hrs
Module 5) Strengthening mechanisms of high-temperature materials, 4 Hrs
Module 6) Basis for development of creep-resistant materials Materials for elevated temperature application - Ni-base superalloys and their applications, High-temperature materials, intermetallics, and their application. 10 Hrs

Course Objective

1 .

To gain understanding of high temperature materials generally exploited at operating temperatures greater than the half of melting temperature.
2 .

To be acquainted with the creep phenomenon and associated mechanisms that primarily decide the thermal capability of the high-temperature materials.

To understand the methods of presentation of creep data and ways of predicting long-time creep properties by performing short-time tests.

To have familiarity with commercially available high temperature materials, their characteristics and applications.

The course outcomes (COs) are as follows:
CO1: Students will gain an understanding of high-temperature materials generally used at operating temperatures greater than half of the melting temperature.
CO2: Students will understand the characteristics and theory of high-temperature materials responsible for sustaining them in severe operating environments and providing resistance to mechanical degradation over extended periods.
CO3:
Students will get an idea about high-temperature tensile, creep, and stress rupture tests and associated mechanisms.

Students will be acquainted with the creep phenomenon, stages of creep, mechanisms of creep, deformation mechanism maps, and associated changes in metallurgical structure.

Students will get knowledge about how to predict the creep without performing a long creep test, the concept of Serby Dorn and Larson - Miller Parameters.

Students will be familiar with the commercially available high-temperature, materials, their special characteristics, and their applications.

CO1: Students will learn the Hilbert space and the Riesz representation theorem.
CO2: They will learn the basics of bounded and unbounded operators.
CO3: They will understand the spectral theorem for compact, self-adjoint, and normal operators.
CO4: They will learn the Banach algebra and its properties.
CO5: They will gain the knowledge of C* algebras and the famous Gelfand-Mazur theorem.
